title: Backward-Compatible Changes
subtopics: Compatibility risks of enums and validation rules
learning_outcomes: Explain how backward-compatible changes affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from adding optional request fields to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on backward-compatible changes in api versioning and lifecycle management. You will connect adding optional request fields to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Backward-Compatible Changes matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying adding optional request fields deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “Backward-Compatible Changes” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Backward-Compatible Changes
content_blocks.code:
/v1/orders/ord_123
/v2/orders/ord_123

# Example migration note:
# v1 deprecated on 2027-06-01; clients should move to v2.
# Publish actual dates only after usage and support policies are reviewed.
content_blocks.expected_output: A version strategy communicates the contract boundary; deprecation needs a timeline, consumer evidence, and migration documentation.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Adding optional request fields”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Adding response properties” and “Compatibility risks of enums and validation rules”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Compatibility is a consumer property; deprecations need evidence, communication, and a migration path. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating backward-compatible changes. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Adding optional request fields” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Backward-Compatible Changes with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating backward-compatible changes as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “Backward-Compatible Changes” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 182: Breaking Changes and Migration.
